comment.value:
The paper presents HC-RefLoCo, a large-scale benchmark designed to address the limitations of existing Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) datasets in the context of large multimodal models (LMMs). By offering over 13,000 images and 44,000 detailed annotations, the benchmark provides a richer and more challenging dataset for evaluating modern REC models. Key features include longer, more detailed referring expressions and multiple evaluation protocols that test accuracy, scale-awareness, and other dimensions of model performance.

Overall, the paper demonstrates solid contributions to the field, with a well-constructed dataset and a comprehensive experimental evaluation involving 24 models. The clarity, originality, and significance of the work make it a valuable resource for advancing REC tasks, though there could be improvements in addressing potential biases in demographic representation and scene diversity.

Dear Reviewer ysoo,

Thank you for your insightful comments. We have carefully considered each of your suggestions. Below, we address your concerns point by point.


**Q1: The annotation lengths spans from around 50 to 150 words. Will it still be suitable for methods that can only take in limited length of expression?**

Modern large multimodal models (LMMs) designed for the referring expression comprehension (REC) task typically rely on large language models (LLMs) as their text encoders to effectively grasp the intricate semantics of referring expressions. LLMs, such as the LLaMA series and Vicuna, have exhibited exceptional language processing capabilities, enabling them to handle extensive text lengths ranging from 2048 tokens to a remarkable 128K tokens (e.g., LLaMA-1: 2048 tokens; LLaMA-2: 4096 tokens; LLaMA-3: 8192 tokens; LLaMA-3.1: 128K tokens). 

In our benchmark, we include referring expressions that span from approximately 50 to 150 words—considerably longer than the typical referring expressions in existing benchmarks, which usually range from 1 to 15 words. Despite this significant increase in length, our expressions remain well within the processing limits of current LLMs. The following table summarizes the text encoders (LLMs) utilized in the REC models evaluated in this work.

Moreover, as demonstrated in Tables 2-3 of the main paper, models utilizing LLMs as text encoders exhibit strong generalization on our benchmark. For example, the state-of-the-art model SPHINX-v2-1k achieves a mAcc of 71.6, highlighting the effectiveness of these models in comprehending lengthy texts, attributed to the superior language compression capabilities of their LLM-based text encoders.

| Model              | Text Encoder                   | 
|:-|:-|
| GroundingGPT [1]   | LEGO-7B                        | 
| Ferret [2]         | Vicuna-7B/13B                  | 
| MiniGPT4-v2 [3]    | LLaMa 2 Chat-7B                | 
| KOSMOS-2 [4]       | KOSMOS-1.3B                    | 
| Shikra [5]         | LLaMA-7B                       | 
| OFA [6]            | BART$_{Base}$-140M             | 
| OFA-Large [6]      | BART$_{Large}$-400M            | 
| Qwen-VL [7]        | Qwen-7B                        | 
| Lenna [8]          | LLaVA-7B                       | 
| ONE PEACE [9]      | Casual Transformer Decoder-4B  | 
| SPHINX-MoE [10]    | Mixtral-8x7B                   | 
| SPHINX [10]        | LLaMA 2-13B                    | 
| SPHINX-1k [10]     | LLaMA 2-13B                    | 
| SPHINX-MoE-1k [10] | Mixtral-8x7B                   | 
| SPHINX-v2-1k [10]  | LLaMA 2-13B                    | 
| PixelLM [11]       | LLaVA-7B/13B                   | 
| LISA [12]          | LLaVA 2-13B                    | 
| PSALM [13]         | Phi 1.5-1.3B                   | 
| GlaMM [14]         | Vicuna-7B                      | 

We agree with you that, many early models, developed prior to the advent of large language models (LLMs), struggled with processing lengthy and intricate texts. This limitation stemmed from their relatively small text encoders, which were not pre-trained on vast datasets of internet-scale language data, resulting in suboptimal comprehension of complex linguistic structures. The objective of this work is to introduce a large-scale, rigorously designed benchmark specifically tailored to challenge contemporary models—24 in total—that utilize LLMs as their text encoders. This benchmark aims to push the boundaries of these advanced models, testing their ability to handle more sophisticated and nuanced textual inputs than what earlier models could manage.

Thank you for your feedback. We will incorporate this discussion into our revision.

**Q2: Clarification on "Distribution of Instance Center"**

In our benchmark, each data sample consists of: 1) an image $I$ with dimensions $W \times H$, where $W$ and $H$ are the width and height of the image, respectively; 2) a target instance $T$, represented by a bounding box $b=(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$, which indicates the target's location within the image $I$. Here, $(x_1, y_1)$ corresponds to the top-left corner of the bounding box $b$, and $(x_2, y_2)$ to the bottom-right corner; 3) a referring expression describing the target $T$. The normalized instance center $c$ is computed as $c=(\frac{|x_1-x_2|}{W}, \frac{|y_1-y_2|}{H})$. As illustrated in Figure 5(b) of the main paper, the distribution of instance centers is depicted as a scatter plot showing all instance centers $\\{c_i\\}_{i=1}^{N}$, where $N$ is the total number of data samples in the benchmark. We will include this clarification into our revised version.

**References**

[1] LEGO: Language enhanced multi-modal grounding model.

[2] Ferret: Refer and ground anything anywhere at any granularity.

[3] MiniGPT-v2: large language model as a unified interface for vision-language multi-task learning.

[4] Kosmos-2: Grounding multimodal large language models to the world.

[5] Shikra: Unleashing multimodal LLM’s referential dialogue magic.

[6] Ofa: Unifying architectures, tasks, and modalities through a simple sequence-to-sequence learning framework.

[7] Qwen-VL: A versatile vision-language model for understanding, localization, text reading, and beyond.

[8] Lenna: Language enhanced reasoning detection assistant.

[9] One-peace: Exploring one general representation model toward unlimited modalities.

[10] SPHINX: The joint mixing of weights, tasks, and visual embeddings for multi-modal large language models.

[11] PixelLM: Pixel reasoning with large multimodal model.

[12] LISA: Reasoning segmentation via large language model.

[13] Psalm: Pixelwise segmentation with large multi-modal model.

[14] GLaMM: Pixel grounding large multimodal model.

title.value: A Large-Scale Human-Centric Benchmark for Referring Expression Comprehension in the LMM Era

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces HC-RefLoCo, a novel benchmark for human-centric referring expression comprehension (REC). HC-RefLoCo challenges large multimodal models with its comprehensive evaluation criteria and unique features. These include a dataset of 13,452 images, 24,129 instances, and 44,738 annotations; detailed annotations averaging 93.2 words from a vocabulary of 18,681 words; sentence-level subject labels; varied instance scales; and multiple evaluation protocols that leverage different IoU criteria and scale-aware assessments.

review.value:
Pros:
1. The work addresses a critical need for more specialized benchmarks in the field of human centric REC. The dataset is large-scale and contains long and detailed descriptions than existing datasets that are derived from general REC datasets.
2. The dataset is diverse, in image size, instance size, and distribution of instance center. The introduction of varied instance scales and multiple evaluation protocols could impact the development and refinement of REC models.
3. The introduction of various IoU criteria and scale-aware evaluations allows for a thorough assessment of model performance across different dimensions.
4. The availability of the benchmark and evaluation code to the public encourages collaboration and further research, broadening the potential impact of the work.
Cons:
1. The annotation lengths spans from around 50 to 150 words. Will it still be suitable for methods that can only take in limited length of expression?
2. Could you explain more about how is 'Distribution of instance center' evaluated?

Dear Reviewer Q7MD,

Thank you for your prompt response and for sharing your insights. 

We would like to elaborate further on the significance of using long referring expressions to identify a person in an image or video:

- *From an Application Perspective:* Consider a scenario where we need to **identify a specific individual** with distinct characteristics from **a large database** containing thousands of images. In this case, we may not have prior knowledge of the image contents, and our only information is the person's distinguishing features. To narrow down the potential search results, it becomes crucial to describe this individual as precisely as possible. Thus, the models need to handle the detailed textual description to locate the target from the database. For instance, in forensic investigations, analysts might use comprehensive descriptions to differentiate a suspect from others in a crowded scene. Similarly, in a search scenario, such as in a photo album application, where the goal is to identify a specific person from a large collection of photos, providing detailed text descriptions can significantly reduce the output space. A brief description like "A man wearing a t-shirt" could yield numerous results if multiple individuals in the album fit that description. In contrast, offering a more detailed and specific description, like "A man in his 30s, wearing a t-shirt and sunglasses, standing on a beach with a mustache," can significantly enhance the accuracy of the search.

- *From a Model Evaluation Perspective:* Large multimodal models today are built on the robust foundation of large language models, which significantly enhances their language comprehension capabilities. However, existing datasets fall short in testing their ability to associate complex linguistic and visual content. For example, in *RefCOCO*, the referring expressions are particularly concise, ranging from single words like "lady" to brief descriptions like "far left person". *RefCOCO+* intentionally excludes locational prepositions (e.g. "far left") commonly found in RefCOCO. The benchmark introduced in this work is designed to more rigorously challenge modern multimodal models.

We recognize that users frequently favor concise descriptions when identifying a target within a given image. This preference, however, primarily applies to **labeling tasks**, where the labeler has direct visual access to both the image and the target, allowing for the use of contextual cues and the target's specific features to generate an efficient description. However, in some realistic scenarios, where users only recognize key characteristics of an individual and need to identify that person from a large database, providing detailed descriptions can be a more effective approach to narrow the search space.

We appreciate your prompt and insightful feedback. We will include these discussions into our revised version. We look forward to further discussions with you.

Thank you for the detailed response. I appreciate the effort to clarify the definitions of "human-centric" and the HC datasets.

I do not complete buy your argument about the task validity. In the example in Figure 1d, if I were tasked with generating a referring expression for the person in the bounding box, I would have just said "second person from the right". Additionally, only one of them has blonde hair in a bun, not three as per your response (the other two are not blonde). While I agree that there may be some ambiguities for the original RefCOCO expressions (shown in the rebuttal pdf), I do not think the solution most people use would be to generate extremely long referring expressions, rather they will add a minimal detail to the expression to resolve the ambiguity and not mention the details that can cause ambiguity -- for example, for the image in Figure 1d, I do not think a person would mention "firefighter" or "certificate" if those details apply to multiple persons in the image. IMO, this dataset is not challenging the model's ability to use the additional details in the description (since only one or few details may actually be needed) but rather the ability of referring expression models to consume long input sequences that may be out-of-distribution.

To make the task seem more valid, I would suggest re-framing the dataset to only include instances where all the included details in the referring expression are actually needed to accurately identify the correct person in the image.

I will keep my score the same.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewers for their time and effort in reviewing our manuscript. In this global response, we primarily address the third comment provided by **Reviewer b3MM**. Please refer to **individual responses** for other questions.

**Reviewer b3MM-Q3: Potential Application of Referring Expression Generation**

We concur that our benchmark can also be effectively utilized for the Referring Expression Generation (REG) task, which involves generating natural language descriptions to uniquely identify a specific object, person, or region within an image. Below, we delve into the evaluation metrics commonly used in the REG task:

- CIDEr and BLEU Scores: These metrics assess the similarity between a REG model's generated expression and a reference expression (i.e., ground truth). Since there are numerous valid ways to describe the same target, relying on a limited set of reference expressions may result in unfair evaluations of alternative but equally valid descriptions. In our work, the reference expressions are detailed and extensive, making CIDEr and BLEU potentially inadequate, particularly for models that generate contextually rich expressions.

- Re-Localization. Some methods, such as DisCLIP [1], use a different evaluation protocol for REG, which we refer to as re-localization. In this protocol, a **REG model** first generates a referring expression $E$ for the target instance. A **pre-trained REC model** is then used to predict a bounding box $B$ based on the generated expression $E$. The expression $E$ is considered accurate if the predicted box $B$ matches the ground-truth box. Following the protocol used in DisCLIP [1] (a closed-source model), we evaluate two open-source models, Ferret [2] and MiniGPT-v2 [3], which are capable of handling the **REG** task, using SPHINX-v2-1k [4] as the **pre-trained REC model** due to its state-of-the-art performance. The results on our benchmark are presented in the table below. In the table, "Ground-Truth" refers to the use of the ground-truth referring expressions, rather than those generated by any model, as input to the pre-trained REC model (SPHINX-v2-1k [4]). This approach is equivalent to using SPHINX-v2-1k [4] directly for the REC task, serving as a performance upper bound.

|REG Model|$mAcc$ (Val)|$mAcc$ (Test)|$mAcc$ (Val+Test)|
|:-|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|Ground-Truth|71.6|71.7|71.7|
|Ferret [2]|49.7|50.2|50.1|
|MiniGPT-v2 [3]|50.3|50.2|50.2|

- GPT-4-as-a-Judge: This approach is inspired by the evaluation methods used for large language models (LLMs). Assessing the quality of an LLM's open-ended responses poses significant challenges, and [5] shows that GPT-4's advanced language comprehension enables it to score any LLM's open-ended response on a scale of 1 to 10, a process termed GPT-4-as-a-Judge. LLaVA [6], Ferret [2] and Ferret-v2 [7] adopt a similar approach for REG evaluation. Here, we introduce a REG evaluation using GPT-4v as the judge. Specifically, the REG model's generated expression $E$, along with the target instance, its corresponding image, and the reference expression (i.e., ground-truth) are input into GPT-4v. GPT-4v is then tasked with determining whether the generated expression $E$ accurately describes the target instance and assigning it a score between 1 and 10. The simplified version of our prompt is as follows:

---

*Task description:*

*You are presented with an image, where a red bounding box highlights the target instance, a referring expression generated by a model that describes the target, and a ground-truth expression that accurately describes the target. Your task is to assign a score between 1 and 10 to the generated referring expression. The factors to consider include relevance, accuracy, detail, unbiasedness, and harmlessness. You may also consult the ground-truth expression as a reference.*

*Image: {image}*

*Generated referring expression: {generated_referring_expression}*

*Ground-truth expression: {ground_truth_expression}*

---

We employ this REG evaluation method to assess Ferret [2] and MiniGPT-v2 [3] on our benchmark, with the results shown in the table below.

|REG Model|GPT-4v Score (Val)|GPT-4v Score (Test)|GPT-4v Score (Val+Test)|
|:-|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|Ferret [2]|4.85|5.17|5.12|
|MiniGPT-v2 [3]|4.53|4.69|4.59|

We will include these discussions and the evaluation metrics related to the application of the REG task in our work.

**References**

[1] DisCLIP: Open-Vocabulary Referring Expression Generation.

[2] Ferret: Refer and Ground Anything Anywhere at Any Granularity.

[3] MiniGPT-v2: Large Language Model as a Unified Interface for Vision-Language Multi-task Learning.

[4] SPHINX: The Joint Mixing of Weights, Tasks, and Visual Embeddings for Multi-modal Large Language Models.

[5] Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena.

[6] Visual Instruction Tuning.

[7] Ferret-v2: An Improved Baseline for Referring and Grounding with Large Language Models.

Thank you for your insightful and constructive comments. We have carefully considered each of your suggestions. Below, we address your concerns point by point.

**Q1: Human and Scene Diversity**

Thanks for your thoughtful feedback. We have conducted an analysis of both human and scene diversity, as detailed below.

- Human Diversity: We use MiVOLO (https://github.com/wildchlamydia/mivolo) to predict the gender and age of each individual, with subsequent manual corrections. The resulting statistics are presented in the following tables, where "unrecognizable" typically refers to cases where faces are either obscured or blurred.

|Male|Female|Unrecognizable|

|8.72\%|12.39\%|51.61\%|12.93\%|14.35\%|

- Scene Diversity: We begin by obtaining the 365 scene categories from the Places365 benchmark, which is the most extensive dataset for scene recognition. Using GPT-4o, we then consolidate these 365 scenes into 20 broader categories. Each image in our benchmark is subsequently processed by GPT-4o to predict its corresponding scene category, followed by a manual correction of the predictions. **Q2: Incorporating Segmentation Annotations**

We appreciate this suggestion. Indeed, some models are capable of predicting masks for target instances. To generate segmentation annotations, we employ a two-step process. Specifically, given a target instance and its corresponding image: 1) we input the image and the target instance’s bounding box into the SAM-2 model to produce an initial mask; 2) we manually review the predicted mask and make corrections if any errors are present. We find that SAM-2's predictions are generally satisfactory, with only a small fraction of challenging cases (2\%) requiring manual correction. The following table presents the evaluation of four models that can predict masks for target instances. It is worthy noting that these four models are also evaluated in the main paper. The evaluation protocols remain consistent with those described in the main paper, except that the IoU is calculated between the predicted mask and the ground-truth mask instead of between the predicted and ground-truth boxes.

rebuttal.value:
Dear Reviewer Q7MD,

Thank you for your insightful comments. We have carefully considered each of your suggestions. Below, we address your concerns point by point.

**Q1: The Validity of the Task**

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We understand your concerns regarding the necessity and realism of long-form referring expressions in our benchmark.

- We agree that shorter expressions may often suffice to identify the correct person in simpler cases. Nevertheless, in real-world applications, especially in complex or crowded scenes, longer descriptions may be necessary to accurately disambiguate between individuals who share similar features or are engaged in similar activities. Consider, for example, the scenario depicted in Figure 1(d) in the main paper, where five individuals are present: (1) all are firefighters dressed in uniforms; (2) four are female; (3) three are holding framed certificates; (4) three have blond hair styled in buns; and (5) only one is holding a frame with both hands. The individual we intend to ground satisfies all five of these properties, whereas the others meet some of the first four criteria. Although it is possible to identify this individual solely by the unique property described in (5), relying on such a minimal cue requires significant cognitive effort for human labelers. A more detailed description, on the other hand, can effectively preclude ambiguity and streamline the identification process.

- To further substantiate our argument, we have included nine illustrative cases from the RefCOCO series in the **rebuttal PDF**. In each of these cases, the provided expression is intended to uniquely identify a specific instance within the image. However, due to the overly concise nature of these descriptions, the expressions fail to serve their intended purpose, instead referring to multiple instances within the scene, leading to unreliable evaluation. This ambiguity underscores the limitations of relying on minimal descriptions and highlights the need for more detailed and contextually rich expressions to ensure accurate identification in complex visual environments.

- Existing LMMs are often constructed on the foundation of LLMs, known for their exceptional language comprehension capabilities. Our intention with including detailed descriptions is to create a more challenging and comprehensive evaluation of these models. Our benchmark tests their proficiency in associating semantically rich texts with intricate visual elements. Furthermore, this paper introduces a broader set of evaluation protocols compared to previous works, ensuring a more thorough and multidimensional analysis of model performance.

**Q2: The Definition of the "Human-Centric" Context**

We apologize for the confusion regarding the term "human-centric" in the introduction. We will revise the introduction to explicitly define "human-centric referring expression comprehension" (HC-REC), which involves correctly grounding a specific human in the image based on the description. 

Specifically, we will include the following revision to replace the definition of the "referring expression comprehension" (REC) task described in *line 32*:

---

*In this work, we focus on a "human-centric" context, which we define as scenarios where the primary task is to correctly identify and ground a specific human subject within an image based on a given textual description. This involves interpreting detailed descriptions related to appearance, actions, interactions, and other contextual cues to accurately pinpoint the intended human within a complex visual scene.*

---

Below, we also provide the structure of the introduction section for reference:

- *L23-27*: We provide a brief overview of the current landscape in human-centric AI, noting that most research has concentrated on single-modality tasks.

- *L27-30*: We underscore the paradigm shift from single-modality to multimodality, driven by the advent of LMMs such as GPT-4V and Google Gemini.

- *L30-35*: We introduce the referring expression comprehension (REC) task, which serves as a representative challenge in the multimodal domain. We articulate the motivation behind our work—developing benchmarks tailored to human-centric REC in the context of the emerging capabilities of LMMs.

- *L36-47*: We critically assess the limitations of the relevant datasets. We clarify the abbreviation "HC" for "human-centric" in line 39 to ensure consistency throughout the paper.

- *L48-81*: This part details the key attributes of our HC-RefLoCo benchmark, highlighting its large scale, the inclusion of extensive annotations, subject labels for evaluating diverse scenarios, comprehensive coverage of varying instance scales, and the introduction of multiple evaluation protocols.

- *L82-86*: We describe our comprehensive evaluation of 24 recent LMMs on our benchmark, demonstrating the benchmark's capacity to provide meaningful insights and comparisons.

**Q3: The Definition of HC-RefCOCO, HC-RefCOCO+ and HC-RefCOCOg**

Thank you for your careful reading of our paper and for raising this question. As outlined in *lines 36-40*, "HC-RefCOCO", "HC-RefCOCO+", and "HC-RefCOCOg" are human-centric Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) benchmarks. These benchmarks are derived from the general REC datasets RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, through a meticulous filtering process that focuses on human-related images and text annotations. Specifically, each instance within the original datasets is categorized, and only those labeled with the "human" category are retained to form the HC-RefCOCO series. 

We acknowledge that the original explanation could have been clearer. To address this, we will revise the relevant sections of the manuscript to provide a more explicit and easily locatable introduction to "HC-RefCOCO", "HC-RefCOCO+", and "HC-RefCOCOg", ensuring that their definitions are more effectively communicated to the reader.

review.value:
While the proposed benchmark, on the whole, seems very soundly designed and evaluated, *I have concerns regarding the validity of the task*. It’s unclear if the long detailed descriptions are actually needed for identifying the correct person. In all the examples in Figure 1 (except 1f), a subset of the referring expression would be sufficient to disambiguate the correct person from all the persons in the scene. What value do long-form referring expressions add if the additional information is not necessary for the task? I don't think they represent a realistic scenario, since people will always provide shorter referring expressions than longer ones, provided that both are sufficient for identifying the correct person. So it seems like the main thing being tested here is the ability of REC models to generalize to longer contexts without training.

Aside from that, I think the benchmark is a solid contribution, and the paper is very well written.

strengths.value:
- The benchmark construction seems sound, and well-designed.
- Excellent analysis of the benchmark, in Figures 3--5. I especially liked the analysis in Figure 5b!
- Experiments and analysis seem fairly thorough, and well-designed.
- Paper is well-writen, and easy to follow.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: - The introduction doesn’t address or define what a “human-centric” context is. It took me till L124 to realize that the task is to correctly ground a specific human in the image based on the description. This is not what I would have intuitively thought “human-centric” meant.

limitations.value: The limitations have been addressed in the supplementary material.

correctness.value: Yes, the claims seem to be correct.

clarity.value: The paper is very clearly written.

relation_to_prior_work.value: Yes, the proposed benchmark is compared to other benchmarks, but it's unclear what exactly they are. Specifically, what are HC-RefCOCO, HC-RefCOCO+ and HC-RefCOCOg? The papers that are cited do not show “HC” anywhere, and I could not find any references on the internet

title.value: This dataset paper introduces HC-RefLoCo, a new benchmark for evaluating large multimodal models in referring expression comprehension (REC) tasks.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper "A Large-Scale Human-Centric Benchmark for Referring Expression Comprehension in the LMM Era" introduces HC-RefLoCo, which addresses the limitations of referring expression comprehension benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg) by providing 13,452 images, 24,129 instances, and 44,738 annotations, with each annotation averaging 93.2 words and covering various subjects like appearance, human-object interaction, location, action, celebrity, and OCR. The annotations are manually reviewed for accuracy.

review.value: I believe this paper's benchmark work has included diverse evaluation protocols, such as accuracy with different IoU criteria, scale-aware evaluation, and subject-specific assessments. Its experiments with 24 models demonstrate HC-RefLoCo’s capability to challenge and advance LMMs by providing detailed and diverse data.

strengths.value:
1. The HC-RefLoCo dataset is thoughtfully designed and well-motivated, which contains a wealth of information, making it a valuable asset for the LMM research community.
2. The benchmark introduced in this paper significantly surpasses existing benchmarks such as RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg in terms of scale. The annotations in HC-RefLoCo are much more detailed and longer. This provides a richer and more comprehensive context for evaluating the performance of LMMs.
3. The benchmark includes various and comprehensive evaluation protocols that go beyond traditional metrics.
4. The paper features a thorough evaluation of several LMMs, offering valuable insights and benchmarks.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- The human and scene diversity in the dataset can be further explored and discussed.
- A brief mention of plans or possibilities for incorporating segmentation annotations in future work would be beneficial.

limitations.value:
- There is insufficient discussion on potential biases in the dataset, such as demographic representation and scene diversity.
- The current annotation only contains bounding boxes. Introducing segmentation annotations could significantly enhance the dataset's utility for more detailed object recognition tasks. 
- The paper currently omits the potential application of Referring Expression Generation (REG) to this benchmark. Including a brief mention of REG's applicability would enhance the benchmark's perceived versatility and potential use cases.

correctness.value: The claims made in the submission appear to be correct. The dataset is constructed in a sound and well-documented manner. As a benchmark, the evaluation methods and experiment design are appropriate and performed correctly, ensuring reliable and reproducible results. The open-source code provided further supports the accuracy and transparency of the findings.

title.value: A Large-Scale Human-Centric Benchmark for Referring Expression Comprehension in the LMM Era

abstract.value: Prior research in human-centric AI has primarily addressed single-modality tasks like pedestrian detection, action recognition, and pose estimation. However, the emergence of large multimodal models (LMMs) such as GPT-4V has redirected attention towards integrating language with visual content. Referring expression comprehension (REC) represents a prime example of this multimodal approach. Current human-centric REC benchmarks, typically sourced from general datasets, fall short in the LMM era due to their limitations, such as insufficient testing samples, overly concise referring expressions, and limited vocabulary, making them inadequate for evaluating the full capabilities of modern REC models. In response, we present HC-RefLoCo (Human-Centric Referring Expression Comprehension with Long Context), a benchmark that includes 13,452 images, 24,129 instances, and 44,738 detailed annotations, encompassing a vocabulary of 18,681 words. Each annotation, meticulously reviewed for accuracy, averages 93.2 words and includes topics such as appearance, human-object interaction, location, action, celebrity, and OCR. HC-RefLoCo provides a wider range of instance scales and diverse evaluation protocols, encompassing accuracy with various IoU criteria, scale-aware evaluation, and subject-specific assessments. Our experiments, which assess 24 models, highlight HC-RefLoCo’s potential to advance human-centric AI by challenging contemporary REC models with comprehensive and varied data. Our benchmark, along with the evaluation code, are available at https://github.com/ZhaoJingjing713/HC-RefLoCo.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
